WHAT IS
LAN PAWANKA?

This is a program of the Pawanka Fund that seeks to strengthen the capacities of Indigenous Peoples around the world.

WE SEEK

To strengthen organizational, technical and governance capacities of Indigenous Peoples.

Specific objectives

To create culturally relevant spaces for collaborative learning.
Generate, share & disseminate experiences
To promote changes to inspire Intercultural Philanthropy

OUR APPROACH

Our work connects different dimensions of Indigenous Peoples' collective strengthening through knowledge, governance, sustainability and intercultural management.

    A SPACE FOR EXCHANGE AND COLLECTIVE LEARNING

    The Africa Partners Exchange Meeting brought together partners to share their organizational journeys, Indigenous knowledge, leadership experiences, and ways of responding to the challenges affecting their communities and territories.

    The meeting focused on three interconnected areas:

    01

    CULTURAL REVITALIZATION

    Language preservation and intergenerational knowledge

    02

    INDIGENOUS FOOD SYSTEMS

    Livelihoods and climate resilience

    03

    INDIGENOUS LEADERSHIP

    Rights, youth and community wellbeing

    Sharing knowledge, stories and experiences

    The first days were dedicated to listening and learning from one another. Organizations shared experiences from different territories, showing how Indigenous communities are strengthening their cultures, protecting their territories, sustaining their livelihoods and responding creatively to climate and social changes.

    Language revitalization, traditional medicine, territorial governance, food sovereignty, youth participation and women's leadership emerged as important dimensions of this shared conversation.

    Rather than presenting a single model, the exchange made visible the diversity of Indigenous ways of organizing and responding to contemporary challenges.

    LISTEN

    From experience to collective reflection

    The exchange continued through presentations, cultural and gastronomic showcases, organizational experiences and conversations around community resilience.

    Partners shared how they are adapting food systems to climate change, creating opportunities for women and youth, defending their territories, revitalizing traditional medicine and combining ancestral knowledge with new technologies. These experiences opened a broader reflection on self-determination, resilience and the role of Indigenous communities in shaping their own futures.

    Building our learning network

    A key moment of the meeting was the presentation of LAN Pawanka and the participatory work around the Collective Strengthening Path (CFC).

    Rather than presenting the tool as a finished product, the session invited partners to reflect together on what makes an Indigenous organization strong. Through group exercises, participants identified elements connected to cultural identity, traditional knowledge, self-determination, trust, leadership, governance, accountability, strategic vision, alliances, innovation and women's empowerment.

    The collective exercise also opened a space to listen to partners' experiences with organizational diagnosis. The CFC was explored not simply as an assessment tool, but as an opportunity for organizations to look at their own journeys, recognize challenges and strengthen their collective understanding.

    Participants contributed observations that will help make the tool clearer, shorter and more culturally relevant to different Indigenous realities.

    Learning from the territory

    The final day moved the exchange beyond the meeting space and into the territory.

    Participants visited a sacred place near the Gotu community, accompanied by local community members, students and elders. The elders shared stories about the spiritual significance of the territory and the relationships between community, nature and worldview. Traditional dances and cultural practices became part of this situated learning experience.

    THE PATH CONTINUES

    A path that continues

    The meeting did not conclude with a single answer. It opened a shared path.

    Across four days, organizations exchanged experiences, questioned their own practices, contributed to the development of LAN Pawanka tools and strengthened relationships with Indigenous partners from different parts of Africa.

    The encounter showed that organizational strengthening can begin with something as fundamental as meeting, listening, sharing knowledge and recognizing the strengths that already exist within communities.

    From Kenya, a collective path began — one rooted in Indigenous knowledge, self-determination, solidarity and the possibility of learning from one another.

    A collective exploration of organizational strength

    What makes an Indigenous organization strong?

    Different voices, shared reflections and collective understandings of organizational strength.

    01 · Kenya partners exchange meeting

    Collective construction of the concept of a strong Indigenous organization

    During the Kenya meeting, participants worked collectively in four groups to reflect on what makes an Indigenous organization strong. Each group developed its own definition, grounded in the ideas and perspectives shared during the exercise.

    02 · Voices from the organizational diagnoses

    Strength, understood from within the organizations

    The diagnostic conversations brought forward the perspectives of Indigenous organizations. Their words speak to different dimensions of organizational strength, from structure and leadership to community priorities and self-determination.

    ORGANIZATION

    “For an organization to be strong means that the organization is well structured, having its different bodies and organs—such as a general assembly, a board of directors, and staff—as well as an office and focal points depending on its size. It must be able to manage in a transparent way.”

    ORGANIZATION

    “A strong organization has a clear vision on what it needs to achieve and a strategic outlook to meet its mission.”

    The interview also highlights autonomy, trusted communication, knowledgeable leadership, community support, networks and alliances.

    ORGANIZATION

    “A strong organization is one that is able to quickly respond to the needs of the people itself, understanding the needs and priorities of the youth you are working with. Because the issues and aspirations keep changing, a strong organization always tries to change to adapt to what their needs are.”

    ORGANIZATION

    “Being an indigenous organization, letting it be community led when it's doing things or projects, anchored in the ethics of the community. Getting to understand the people you are working with and when it comes to activities let them lead, I think that is one thing that will make an organization stand out.”

    ORGANIZATION

    “Participatory approaches and letting the community be the one leading are essential; therefore, we ask for the free, prior, and informed consent from them, and we consult with them because we know the communities have priority.”

    ORGANIZATION

    “From my perspective, a strong organization means that you are capable of really supporting your constituents or the groups that you work with, and that you are able to interest your partners or your allies to network with you and support you along the way.”

    Different experiences, different voices — woven together without losing what makes each one unique.

    LAN PAWANKA AFRICA · Pawanka Fund

    THE STORY BEHIND LAN PAWANKA

    LAN PAWANKA emerged from more than eleven years of collaboration between the Pawanka Fund and Indigenous organizations across the world’s seven sociocultural regions. Throughout this journey, shared experiences, lessons learned, and organizational priorities revealed the need for a capacity-strengthening program designed by and for Indigenous Peoples.

    To shape this vision collectively, Pawanka conducted a participatory organizational diagnosis with a representative group of strategic partners from the world’s seven sociocultural regions. Selected through a collaborative process to reflect the diversity of Indigenous organizational realities, these partners contributed their experiences through 38 virtual interviews and the co-creation of a culturally relevant diagnostic tool covering governance, strategic planning, financial and administrative management, project implementation, external relations, and organizational capacity strengthening. The process was guided by the Fund’s principles of self-determination, reciprocity, interculturality, solidarity, and intergenerational knowledge transmission.

    The organizational diagnosis identified the cultural identity, ancestral knowledge, and community governance systems of Indigenous organizations as their greatest strengths, recognizing them as the foundation of organizational legitimacy, collective cohesion, and resilience. Nearly three-quarters (73%) of participating organizations reported consensus-based decision-making, demonstrating the continued strength of Indigenous governance across diverse contexts.

    The diagnosis also revealed common structural challenges that continue to affect many Indigenous organizations, including high dependence on external funding (more than 80%), limited institutional memory due to the absence of systematic knowledge management mechanisms (91%), fragmented document management systems that increase the risk of information loss (55%), digital capacity gaps related to connectivity and technical skills (73%), and the need to strengthen the meaningful participation of women, youth, and traditional knowledge holders in leadership and decision-making processes (55%).

    These collective findings became the foundation of LAN PAWANKA. In response to the priorities identified through the organizational diagnosis, the program was designed as a multi-level learning model that combines practical tools, peer exchange, mentoring, and intercultural learning processes to strengthen Indigenous organizations while building on their own knowledge systems, governance practices, and cultural strengths.
